14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199:

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231:

234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES
235: 
236: ### Create Reference File When
237: 
238: **Workflow Complexity**:
239: - Multi-phase workflows with validation checkpoints
240: - Decision trees with multiple branches
241: - Pattern libraries with 5+ variations
242: - Systematic debugging procedures
243: 
244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes
249: 
250: **Size Threshold**:
251: - Content exceeds 200 lines
252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed
254: 
255: ### Keep in SKILL.md When
256: 
257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
261:   > **Note**: RULES sections in SKILL.md use ALL-CAPS H3 headers: `### ALWAYS`, `### NEVER`, `### ESCALATE IF` (or `####` at phase depth). See [skill-md-template.md](./skill-md-template.md) for the complete pattern.
262: - Quick reference
263: 
264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines
265: 
266: ### Reference File Types for AI Agent Skills
267: 
268: | Type                | Purpose                                | Example (kebab-case)          | Size           |
269: | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- |
270: | **Workflow**        | Multi-phase processes with checkpoints | `implementation-workflows.md` | 500-1500 lines |
271: | **Pattern Library** | Code patterns with before/after        | `shared-patterns.md`          | 300-800 lines  |
272: | **Standards**       | Rules and conventions                  | `code-quality-standards.md`   | 400-1000 lines |

275: | **Quick Reference** | Commands, shortcuts, checklists        | `quick-reference.md`          | 200-400 lines  |
276: 
277: **Note:** All authored reference file names use kebab-case (hyphens, lowercase).

281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown

292:

294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296:

298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]

301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```

306: **Examples from Real Skills**:

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882: 
883: ---
884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"
1073:

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.

73: #### GOOD Intro Structure

75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```

101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.

103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!

115: 
116: ### Core Principle

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.

281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
300: 
301: ### Core Principle

303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```

306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"
309: - "Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history"
310: 
311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312: 
313: **Purpose**: Structured processes with mandatory checkpoints
314: 
315: **Format**:
316: ```markdown
317: ### The [Number] Phases
318: 
319: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
320: 
321: #### Phase 1: [Phase Name]
322: 
323: **Purpose**: [What this phase accomplishes]
324: 
325: **Actions**:
326: 1. [Action 1]

328: 
329: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`

332: 
333: [Similar structure]
334: ```

337: - **"You MUST complete"** - Mandatory language
338: - **Named checkpoints** - `checkpoint_name` for validation
339: - **Sequential phases** - Cannot skip ahead

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882:

884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006:

1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"

14: 
15: Copy-paste boundary templates, naming conventions, deterministic recipes, and Cargo commands for Rust development in OpenCode.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: Provides the rustdoc block and the Cargo, formatting, build and supply-chain commands needed to take a Rust crate through its release gate.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Writing rustdoc for a new public operation
28: - Setting up workspace, rustfmt or Clippy baselines
29: - Running the build and verification gate for a core, native, WASM or WASI target
30: - Checking feature isolation or supply-chain gates
31: 
32: ---
33: 
34: ## 2. RUSTDOC TEMPLATE
35: 
36: ```rust
37: /// Canonicalizes records for JavaScript serialization.
38: ///
39: /// Output keys are ordered lexically and scores use the operation-specific
40: /// six-decimal quantizer. These rules protect serialized-output and numeric
41: /// parity with the TypeScript oracle.
42: ///
43: /// # Errors
44: ///
45: /// Returns [`CoreError::NonFiniteScore`] when a score is `NaN` or infinite.
46: /// Returns [`CoreError::DuplicateId`] when deterministic IDs collide.
47: ///
48: /// # Panics
49: ///
50: /// This function does not panic for validated boundary input.
51: ///
52: /// # Examples
53: ///
54: /// ```
55: /// use ranking_core::{canonicalize, CanonicalizeRequestDto};
56: ///
57: /// # fn run() -> Result<(), ranking_core::CoreError> {
58: /// let request = CanonicalizeRequestDto {
59: ///     records: Vec::new(),
60: /// };
61: /// let output = canonicalize(request)?;
62: /// assert!(output.records.is_empty());
63: /// # Ok(())
64: /// # }
65: /// # run()?;
66: /// # Ok::<(), ranking_core::CoreError>(())
67: /// ```
68: pub fn canonicalize(
69:     request: CanonicalizeRequestDto,
70: ) -> Result<CanonicalizeOutputDto, CoreError> {
71:     // ...
72: }
73: ```
74: 
75: For unsafe APIs, also document the caller obligations:
76: 
77: ```rust
78: /// Copies `length` initialized bytes from `pointer`.
79: ///
80: /// # Safety
81: ///
82: /// `pointer` must be non-null and valid for reads of `length` initialized
83: /// bytes. The region must remain alive and immutable for the duration of the
84: /// call, and `length` must not exceed `isize::MAX`.
85: pub unsafe fn copy_foreign_bytes(
86:     pointer: *const u8,
87:     length: usize,
88: ) -> Result<Vec<u8>, BoundaryError> {
89:     // ...
90: }
91: ```
92: 
93: Public boundary documentation states:
94: 
95: - Ownership and copy behavior
96: - Stable JavaScript error code and shape
97: - Synchronous throw versus Promise rejection behavior
98: - Comparator chain or deterministic-ID preimage where observable
99: - Serialization and map ordering
100: - The parity or interop contract protected
101: 
102: ---
103: 
104: ## 3. CARGO AND BUILD QUICK REFERENCE
105: 
106: ### Workspace Baseline
107: 
108: ```toml
109: # Cargo.toml
110: [workspace]
111: resolver = "3"
112: members = ["crates/core", "crates/napi", "crates/wasm"]
113: 
114: [workspace.package]
115: edition = "2024"
116: rust-version = "1.85"
117: license = "MIT"
118: 
119: [workspace.lints.rust]
120: unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn = "deny"
121: 
122: [workspace.lints.clippy]
123: unwrap_used = "deny"
124: expect_used = "deny"
125: panic = "deny"
126: float_cmp = "deny"
127: as_conversions = "deny"
128: indexing_slicing = "deny"
129: 
130: [profile.release]
131: overflow-checks = true
132: lto = "thin"
133: codegen-units = 1
134: ```
135: 
136: Each member opts into workspace policy:
137: 
138: ```toml
139: [package]
140: name = "ranking-core"
141: version = "0.1.0"
142: edition.workspace = true
143: rust-version.workspace = true
144: license.workspace = true
145: 
146: [lints]
147: workspace = true
148: ```
149: 
150: ### rustfmt Baseline
151: 
152: ```toml
153: # rustfmt.toml
154: edition = "2024"
155: style_edition = "2024"
156: max_width = 100
157: newline_style = "Unix"
158: ```
159: 
160: ### Complete Gate Sequence
161: 
162: ```bash
163: cargo fmt --all -- --check
164: cargo check --workspace --all-targets --locked
165: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
166: cargo test --workspace --locked
167: RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked
168: cargo build --workspace --release --locked
169: cargo deny check
170: cargo audit
171: ```
172: 
173: Run the complete sequence before claiming the Rust workspace is verified.
174: 
175: ### Advisory Clippy Review
176: 
177: ```bash
178: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- \
179:   -W clippy::pedantic \
180:   -W clippy::nursery
181: ```
182: 
183: Pedantic and nursery findings are advisory. Promote stable, relevant individual lints instead of denying either group wholesale.
184: 
185: ### Core and Native Targets
186: 
187: ```bash
188: # Pure core
189: cargo test -p ranking-core --locked
190: 
191: # Host native addon
192: cargo build -p ranking-napi --release --locked
193: 
194: # Explicit native target
195: cargo build -p ranking-napi \
196:   --release \
197:   --locked \
198:   --target aarch64-apple-darwin
199: ```
200: 
201: Use the lowest proven Node-API level supporting the required APIs. Test the oldest declared Node version and every published OS, CPU, and libc package.
202: 
203: ### wasm-bindgen Target
204: 
205: ```bash
206: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
207: 
208: cargo build -p ranking-wasm \
209:   --release \
210:   --locked \
211:   --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
212: 
213: wasm-bindgen \
214:   --target nodejs \
215:   --out-dir dist/wasm \
216:   target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/ranking_wasm.wasm
217: ```
218: 
219: Use this target only for an intentionally distinct wasm-bindgen ABI.
220: 
221: ### napi-rs WASI Target
222: 
223: ```bash
224: rustup target add wasm32-wasip1-threads
225: 
226: cargo build -p ranking-napi \
227:   --release \
228:   --locked \
229:   --target wasm32-wasip1-threads
230: ```
231: 
232: Prefer napi-rs's generated WASI fallback when native and WASI must preserve the same Node-facing addon API.
233: 
234: ### Feature Isolation
235: 
236: ```bash
237: cargo check -p ranking-core --no-default-features --locked
238: cargo check -p ranking-napi --no-default-features --features native-addon --locked
239: cargo check -p ranking-wasm --no-default-features --features wasm --locked
240: ```
241: 
242: ### Supply-Chain Gates
243: 
244: ```bash
245: cargo deny check
246: cargo audit
247: cargo vet --locked
248: ```
249: 
250: `cargo deny` and `cargo audit` are blocking when configured. Record `cargo vet` status while policy is advisory, then make it blocking after criteria, imports, and exceptions are committed.
251:

11: ---
12: 
13: # Commenting & Rustdoc Rules
14: 
15: Formatting standards, naming conventions, and TypeScript interoperability rules for Rust files in the OpenCode development environment.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: Sets the comment and rustdoc rules that let a reviewer recover intent, safety preconditions and the protected parity contract from the code itself.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Writing or reviewing comments in Rust source
28: - Adding a `// SAFETY:` justification around an unsafe block
29: - Drafting rustdoc for a public or boundary operation
30: - Suppressing a lint and recording the reason
31: 
32: ---
33: 
34: ## 2. COMMENTING AND RUSTDOC RULES
35: 
36: ### Comment Principles
37: 
38: 1. Explain durable constraints, invariants, and tradeoffs.
39: 2. Explain WHY the code differs from an obvious alternative.
40: 3. Name the parity, ownership, safety, or error contract protected.
41: 4. Do not restate syntax or mechanics.
42: 5. Do not keep commented-out code.
43: 6. Do not embed transient packet, task, checklist, ADR, ticket, or spec-folder identifiers.
44: 7. Keep comments accurate when behavior changes.
45: 
46: ### Comment Examples
47: 
48: ```rust
49: // The identifier is the terminal key so equal scores never inherit input order.
50: candidates.sort_by(compare_candidates);
51: 
52: // Normalize negative zero because the JavaScript wire contract emits positive zero.
53: let score = if score == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { score };
54: 
55: // Copy before scheduling because JavaScript retains ownership of the source buffer.
56: let owned_input = input.to_vec();
57: ```
58: 
59: Avoid comments that narrate mechanics:
60: 
61: ```rust
62: // Sort the candidates.
63: candidates.sort_by(compare_candidates);
64: 
65: // Convert the input into a vector.
66: let owned_input = input.to_vec();
67: ```
68: 
69: ### Capitalization
70: 
71: Comment prose starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation when it is a complete sentence.
72: 
73: Exceptions include:
74: 
75: - `rustfmt` directives
76: - `clippy` lint names
77: - Code identifiers at the beginning of a fragment
78: - Standard tags such as `TODO`, when the repository permits them
79: - `// SAFETY:` invariants
80: 
81: ### `// SAFETY:` Comments
82: 
83: Every allowed unsafe block requires an adjacent `// SAFETY:` comment describing all relevant assumptions:
84: 
85: - Pointer validity
86: - Length and alignment
87: - Initialization
88: - Aliasing
89: - Lifetime
90: - Ownership
91: - Cleanup responsibility
92: - Thread affinity
93: 
94: ```rust
95: fn copy_bytes(pointer: *const u8, length: usize) -> Vec<u8> {
96:     assert!(!pointer.is_null() || length == 0);
97: 
98:     // SAFETY: A non-null pointer is required for non-empty input, the caller
99:     // guarantees `length` initialized bytes, and the bytes are copied before
100:     // this function returns, so no borrowed view escapes.
101:     let bytes = unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(pointer, length) };
102: 
103:     bytes.to_vec()
104: }
105: ```
106: 
107: This pattern belongs only in a reviewed boundary crate. The pure core uses `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.
108: 
109: An unsafe block also requires:
110: 
111: - A test exercising the valid path
112: - A test challenging enforceable preconditions
113: - Boundary documentation stating ownership and lifetime
114: - Review of cleanup and thread-affinity behavior
115: 
116: ### Rustdoc Scope
117: 
118: Document all public boundary types and operations. Document private items when their invariants are not obvious from types and names.
119: 
120: Use:
121: 
122: - `//!` for crate and module documentation
123: - `///` for item documentation
124: - Markdown headings for contract sections
125: - Compilable examples
126: - Intra-doc links where practical
127: 
128: ### Public Operation Template
129: 
130: ```rust
131: /// Parses and validates a stable symbol identifier.
132: ///
133: /// The identifier is normalized once and then used as part of the
134: /// deterministic hash preimage.
135: ///
136: /// # Errors
137: ///
138: /// Returns [`SymbolIdError`] when `value` is empty or contains an unsupported
139: /// character.
140: ///
141: /// # Examples
142: ///
143: /// ```
144: /// # use std::error::Error;
145: /// #
146: /// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
147: /// let id = SymbolId::try_from("memory.search")?;
148: /// assert_eq!(id.as_str(), "memory.search");
149: /// # Ok(())
150: /// # }
151: /// #
152: /// # #[derive(Debug)]
153: /// # struct SymbolId(String);
154: /// #
155: /// # impl SymbolId {
156: /// #     fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
157: /// #         &self.0
158: /// #     }
159: /// # }
160: /// #
161: /// # #[derive(Debug)]
162: /// # struct SymbolIdError;
163: /// #
164: /// # impl std::fmt::Display for SymbolIdError {
165: /// #     fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
166: /// #         formatter.write_str("invalid symbol identifier")
167: /// #     }
168: /// # }
169: /// #
170: /// # impl Error for SymbolIdError {}
171: /// #
172: /// # impl TryFrom<&str> for SymbolId {
173: /// #     type Error = SymbolIdError;
174: /// #
175: /// #     fn try_from(value: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
176: /// #         if value.is_empty() {
177: /// #             Err(SymbolIdError)
178: /// #         } else {
179: /// #             Ok(Self(value.to_owned()))
180: /// #         }
181: /// #     }
182: /// # }
183: /// ```
184: pub fn parse_symbol_id(value: &str) -> Result<SymbolId, SymbolIdError> {
185:     SymbolId::try_from(value)
186: }
187: 
188: #[derive(Debug)]
189: pub struct SymbolId(String);
190: 
191: impl SymbolId {
192:     pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
193:         &self.0
194:     }
195: }
196: 
197: #[derive(Debug)]
198: pub struct SymbolIdError;
199: 
200: impl std::fmt::Display for SymbolIdError {
201:     fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
202:         formatter.write_str("invalid symbol identifier")
203:     }
204: }
205: 
206: impl std::error::Error for SymbolIdError {}
207: 
208: impl TryFrom<&str> for SymbolId {
209:     type Error = SymbolIdError;
210: 
211:     fn try_from(value: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
212:         if value.is_empty() {
213:             Err(SymbolIdError)
214:         } else {
215:             Ok(Self(value.to_owned()))
216:         }
217:     }
218: }
219: ```
220: 
221: Examples for fallible operations use `?`, not `unwrap` or `expect`.
222: 
223: ### Required Rustdoc Sections
224: 
225: Use exact standard headings where applicable:
226: 
227: - `# Errors` for fallible public operations
228: - `# Panics` when a public operation can panic
229: - `# Safety` for every `unsafe fn`
230: - `# Examples` for public operations and non-obvious public types
231: 
232: Do not add `# Panics` merely to say a function never panics. Prefer an API whose signature and implementation avoid panic paths.
233: 
234: ### Boundary Documentation
235: 
236: Every exported napi-rs, WASM, WASI, or sidecar operation documents:
237: 
238: - Input ownership and copy behavior
239: - Output ownership
240: - JavaScript error code and shape
241: - Synchronous throw versus Promise rejection
242: - Numeric normalization behavior
243: - Complete comparator or hash preimage when relevant
244: - Serialization and key order when observable
245: - The parity or interop contract protected
246: 
247: Example:
248: 
249: ```rust
250: /// Ranks candidates using the canonical TypeScript comparator.
251: ///
252: /// Input strings and candidate records are copied before native worker

13: # Commenting & Rustdoc Rules
14: 
15: Formatting standards, naming conventions, and TypeScript interoperability rules for Rust files in the OpenCode development environment.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: Sets the comment and rustdoc rules that let a reviewer recover intent, safety preconditions and the protected parity contract from the code itself.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Writing or reviewing comments in Rust source
28: - Adding a `// SAFETY:` justification around an unsafe block
29: - Drafting rustdoc for a public or boundary operation
30: - Suppressing a lint and recording the reason
31: 
32: ---
33: 
34: ## 2. COMMENTING AND RUSTDOC RULES
35: 
36: ### Comment Principles
37: 
38: 1. Explain durable constraints, invariants, and tradeoffs.
39: 2. Explain WHY the code differs from an obvious alternative.
40: 3. Name the parity, ownership, safety, or error contract protected.
41: 4. Do not restate syntax or mechanics.
42: 5. Do not keep commented-out code.
43: 6. Do not embed transient packet, task, checklist, ADR, ticket, or spec-folder identifiers.
44: 7. Keep comments accurate when behavior changes.
45: 
46: ### Comment Examples
47: 
48: ```rust
49: // The identifier is the terminal key so equal scores never inherit input order.
50: candidates.sort_by(compare_candidates);
51: 
52: // Normalize negative zero because the JavaScript wire contract emits positive zero.
53: let score = if score == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { score };
54: 
55: // Copy before scheduling because JavaScript retains ownership of the source buffer.
56: let owned_input = input.to_vec();
57: ```
58: 
59: Avoid comments that narrate mechanics:
60: 
61: ```rust
62: // Sort the candidates.
63: candidates.sort_by(compare_candidates);
64: 
65: // Convert the input into a vector.
66: let owned_input = input.to_vec();
67: ```
68: 
69: ### Capitalization
70: 
71: Comment prose starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation when it is a complete sentence.
72: 
73: Exceptions include:
74: 
75: - `rustfmt` directives
76: - `clippy` lint names
77: - Code identifiers at the beginning of a fragment
78: - Standard tags such as `TODO`, when the repository permits them
79: - `// SAFETY:` invariants
80: 
81: ### `// SAFETY:` Comments
82: 
83: Every allowed unsafe block requires an adjacent `// SAFETY:` comment describing all relevant assumptions:
84: 
85: - Pointer validity
86: - Length and alignment
87: - Initialization
88: - Aliasing
89: - Lifetime
90: - Ownership
91: - Cleanup responsibility
92: - Thread affinity
93: 
94: ```rust
95: fn copy_bytes(pointer: *const u8, length: usize) -> Vec<u8> {
96:     assert!(!pointer.is_null() || length == 0);
97: 
98:     // SAFETY: A non-null pointer is required for non-empty input, the caller
99:     // guarantees `length` initialized bytes, and the bytes are copied before
100:     // this function returns, so no borrowed view escapes.
101:     let bytes = unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(pointer, length) };
102: 
103:     bytes.to_vec()
104: }
105: ```
106: 
107: This pattern belongs only in a reviewed boundary crate. The pure core uses `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.
108: 
109: An unsafe block also requires:
110: 
111: - A test exercising the valid path
112: - A test challenging enforceable preconditions
113: - Boundary documentation stating ownership and lifetime
114: - Review of cleanup and thread-affinity behavior
115: 
116: ### Rustdoc Scope
117: 
118: Document all public boundary types and operations. Document private items when their invariants are not obvious from types and names.
119: 
120: Use:
121: 
122: - `//!` for crate and module documentation
123: - `///` for item documentation
124: - Markdown headings for contract sections
125: - Compilable examples
126: - Intra-doc links where practical
127: 
128: ### Public Operation Template
129: 
130: ```rust
131: /// Parses and validates a stable symbol identifier.
132: ///
133: /// The identifier is normalized once and then used as part of the
134: /// deterministic hash preimage.
135: ///
136: /// # Errors
137: ///
138: /// Returns [`SymbolIdError`] when `value` is empty or contains an unsupported
139: /// character.
140: ///
141: /// # Examples
142: ///
143: /// ```
144: /// # use std::error::Error;
145: /// #
146: /// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
147: /// let id = SymbolId::try_from("memory.search")?;
148: /// assert_eq!(id.as_str(), "memory.search");
149: /// # Ok(())
150: /// # }
151: /// #
152: /// # #[derive(Debug)]
153: /// # struct SymbolId(String);
154: /// #
155: /// # impl SymbolId {
156: /// #     fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
157: /// #         &self.0
158: /// #     }
159: /// # }
160: /// #
161: /// # #[derive(Debug)]
162: /// # struct SymbolIdError;
163: /// #
164: /// # impl std::fmt::Display for SymbolIdError {
165: /// #     fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
166: /// #         formatter.write_str("invalid symbol identifier")
167: /// #     }
168: /// # }
169: /// #
170: /// # impl Error for SymbolIdError {}
171: /// #
172: /// # impl TryFrom<&str> for SymbolId {
173: /// #     type Error = SymbolIdError;
174: /// #
175: /// #     fn try_from(value: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
176: /// #         if value.is_empty() {
177: /// #             Err(SymbolIdError)
178: /// #         } else {
179: /// #             Ok(Self(value.to_owned()))
180: /// #         }
181: /// #     }
182: /// # }
183: /// ```
184: pub fn parse_symbol_id(value: &str) -> Result<SymbolId, SymbolIdError> {
185:     SymbolId::try_from(value)
186: }
187: 
188: #[derive(Debug)]
189: pub struct SymbolId(String);
190: 
191: impl SymbolId {
192:     pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
193:         &self.0
194:     }
195: }
196: 
197: #[derive(Debug)]
198: pub struct SymbolIdError;
199: 
200: impl std::fmt::Display for SymbolIdError {
201:     fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
202:         formatter.write_str("invalid symbol identifier")
203:     }
204: }
205: 
206: impl std::error::Error for SymbolIdError {}
207: 
208: impl TryFrom<&str> for SymbolId {
209:     type Error = SymbolIdError;
210: 
211:     fn try_from(value: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
212:         if value.is_empty() {
213:             Err(SymbolIdError)
214:         } else {
215:             Ok(Self(value.to_owned()))
216:         }
217:     }
218: }
219: ```
220: 
221: Examples for fallible operations use `?`, not `unwrap` or `expect`.
222: 
223: ### Required Rustdoc Sections
224: 
225: Use exact standard headings where applicable:
226: 
227: - `# Errors` for fallible public operations
228: - `# Panics` when a public operation can panic
229: - `# Safety` for every `unsafe fn`
230: - `# Examples` for public operations and non-obvious public types
231: 
232: Do not add `# Panics` merely to say a function never panics. Prefer an API whose signature and implementation avoid panic paths.
233: 
234: ### Boundary Documentation
235: 
236: Every exported napi-rs, WASM, WASI, or sidecar operation documents:
237: 
238: - Input ownership and copy behavior
239: - Output ownership
240: - JavaScript error code and shape
241: - Synchronous throw versus Promise rejection
242: - Numeric normalization behavior
243: - Complete comparator or hash preimage when relevant
244: - Serialization and key order when observable
245: - The parity or interop contract protected
246: 
247: Example:
248: 
249: ```rust
250: /// Ranks candidates using the canonical TypeScript comparator.
251: ///
252: /// Input strings and candidate records are copied before native worker
253: /// execution. Invalid input rejects the returned Promise with code
254: /// `INVALID_INPUT`. Equal scores are ordered by identifier and then source
255: /// index, protecting stable sort and serialized-output parity.
256: ```
257: 
258: ### Lint Suppressions
259: 
260: Lint suppressions require a durable reason and the narrowest possible scope.
261: 
262: ```rust
263: #[allow(clippy::cast_precision_loss)]
264: fn age_as_score_input(age_seconds: u32) -> f64 {
265:     // Every u32 value is exactly representable in an f64 mantissa.
266:     f64::from(age_seconds)
267: }
268: ```
269: 
270: Do not add crate-wide `allow` attributes to silence ordinary quality findings.
271:

13: # Formatting Rules & Import/Module Ordering
14: 
15: Formatting standards, naming conventions, and TypeScript interoperability rules for Rust files in the OpenCode development environment.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: Fixes the rustfmt baseline, numeric literal style and import and module ordering that make Rust source mechanically reviewable and its collection output deterministic.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Formatting Rust source or configuring rustfmt
28: - Writing numeric literals or parity helper expressions
29: - Ordering imports, module declarations, re-exports or macros
30: - Reviewing deterministic collection formatting and sorting
31: 
32: ---
33: 
34: ## 2. FORMATTING RULES
35: 
36: ### rustfmt Is Authoritative
37: 
38: All Rust code MUST be formatted by the workspace-pinned `rustfmt`.
39: 
40: ```bash
41: cargo fmt --all
42: cargo fmt --all --check
43: ```
44: 
45: Do not hand-format code against `rustfmt`. If formatting is unsuitable, simplify the code before adding formatter overrides.
46: 
47: ### Indentation
48: 
49: - **Size**: 4 spaces
50: - **Tabs**: Never use literal tabs in source
51: - **Continuation**: Let `rustfmt` determine continuation indentation
52: 
53: ### Braces
54: 
55: Use standard Rust brace placement:
56: 
57: ```rust
58: if condition {
59:     run_primary();
60: } else {
61:     run_fallback();
62: }
63: 
64: fn run_primary() {}
65: 
66: fn run_fallback() {}
67: ```
68: 
69: ### Semicolons
70: 
71: Use semicolons for statements and omit the semicolon from an expression intentionally returned from a block.
72: 
73: ```rust
74: fn doubled(value: u32) -> u32 {
75:     value * 2
76: }
77: 
78: fn record(value: u32, output: &mut Vec<u32>) {
79:     output.push(value);
80: }
81: ```
82: 
83: Do not add `return` solely to avoid understanding a short tail expression. Use explicit `return` for early exits.
84: 
85: ```rust
86: fn normalize(value: f64) -> Result<f64, &'static str> {
87:     if !value.is_finite() {
88:         return Err("value must be finite");
89:     }
90: 
91:     Ok(value)
92: }
93: ```
94: 
95: ### Line Length
96: 
97: - Follow the workspace `rustfmt` configuration.
98: - Prefer source that remains readable near 100 characters.
99: - Allow formatter-controlled exceptions for URLs, generated names, and signatures that become less readable when manually decomposed.
100: - Do not use `#[rustfmt::skip]` for ordinary handwritten code.
101: 
102: ### Trailing Commas
103: 
104: Use trailing commas in multiline structs, enums, calls, arrays, tuples, and parameter lists.
105: 
106: ```rust
107: struct SearchConfig {
108:     query: String,
109:     limit: u32,
110:     include_metadata: bool,
111: }
112: 
113: fn search(
114:     config: &SearchConfig,
115:     candidates: &[Candidate],
116: ) -> Result<Vec<Candidate>, SearchError> {
117:     Ok(candidates.to_vec())
118: }
119: 
120: #[derive(Clone)]
121: struct Candidate;
122: 
123: #[derive(Debug)]
124: struct SearchError;
125: ```
126: 
127: ### Multiline Types
128: 
129: Break complex types at logical boundaries. Introduce a descriptive type alias when it clarifies a domain concept rather than merely shortening a line.
130: 
131: ```rust
132: use std::collections::BTreeMap;
133: 
134: type RankedByGroup = BTreeMap<String, Vec<RankedCandidate>>;
135: 
136: #[derive(Debug)]
137: struct RankedCandidate {
138:     id: String,
139:     score: f64,
140: }
141: 
142: fn group_ranked_candidates(
143:     candidates: impl IntoIterator<Item = RankedCandidate>,
144: ) -> RankedByGroup {
145:     let mut grouped = BTreeMap::new();
146: 
147:     for candidate in candidates {
148:         grouped
149:             .entry(candidate.id.clone())
150:             .or_insert_with(Vec::new)
151:             .push(candidate);
152:     }
153: 
154:     grouped
155: }
156: ```
157: 
158: ### Match Formatting
159: 
160: Prefer exhaustive `match` expressions for boundary-relevant enums and errors.
161: 
162: ```rust
163: enum CoreError {
164:     InvalidInput,
165:     NonFiniteScore,
166:     InternalInvariant,
167: }
168: 
169: fn error_code(error: &CoreError) -> &'static str {
170:     match error {
171:         CoreError::InvalidInput => "INVALID_INPUT",
172:         CoreError::NonFiniteScore => "NON_FINITE_SCORE",
173:         CoreError::InternalInvariant => "INTERNAL_INVARIANT",
174:     }
175: }
176: ```
177: 
178: Do not add a wildcard arm merely to silence a new variant in an adapter. Exhaustive matching protects JavaScript error-code parity.
179: 
180: ### Numeric Literals
181: 
182: Use separators when they clarify scale:
183: 
184: ```rust
185: const MICROS_PER_UNIT: f64 = 1_000_000.0;
186: const MAX_SAFE_INTEGER: u64 = 9_007_199_254_740_991;
187: ```
188: 
189: Do not use magic constants for parity-sensitive operations. Name the scale, radix, delimiter, truncation length, and algorithm parameters.
190: 
191: ### Deterministic Collection Formatting
192: 
193: Use canonical collection types when order is observable:
194: 
195: ```rust
196: use std::collections::BTreeMap;
197: 
198: fn canonical_metadata() -> BTreeMap<String, String> {
199:     BTreeMap::from([
200:         ("kind".to_owned(), "memory".to_owned()),
201:         ("state".to_owned(), "active".to_owned()),
202:     ])
203: }
204: ```
205: 
206: Do not rely on `HashMap` or `HashSet` iteration for:
207: 
208: - Serialized output
209: - Hash preimages
210: - Deterministic identifiers
211: - Ranking or traversal
212: - Snapshot text
213: - JavaScript-visible arrays
214: - Diagnostic output covered by golden fixtures
215: 
216: ### Sorting Rules
217: 
218: Every observable sort MUST use a complete comparator with a deterministic unique terminal key.
219: 
220: ```rust
221: use std::cmp::Ordering;
222: 
223: #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
224: struct RankedCandidate {
225:     id: String,
226:     score: f64,
227:     source_index: u32,
228: }
229: 
230: fn sort_candidates(candidates: &mut [RankedCandidate]) {
231:     candidates.sort_by(|left, right| {
232:         right
233:             .score
234:             .total_cmp(&left.score)
235:             .then_with(|| left.id.cmp(&right.id))
236:             .then_with(|| left.source_index.cmp(&right.source_index))
237:     });
238: }
239: ```
240: 
241: Requirements:
242: 
243: - Reject non-finite values before sorting unless their order is explicitly contracted.
244: - Do not use `partial_cmp(...).unwrap()`.
245: - Do not use `sort_unstable*` for parity-visible output.
246: - Do not treat stable input order as the terminal tie-break.
247: - Verify lexical ordering against the permitted TypeScript identifier alphabet.
248: - Do not assume Rust `str::cmp` is equivalent to locale-sensitive JavaScript comparison.
249: 
250: ### Numeric Parity Helpers
251: 
252: Keep distinct TypeScript operations in distinct helpers.
253: 
254: ```rust
255: const SIX_DECIMAL_SCALE: f64 = 1_000_000.0;
256: 
257: fn round_scaled_six(value: f64) -> Result<f64, &'static str> {
258:     if !value.is_finite() {
259:         return Err("value must be finite");
260:     }
261: 
262:     let rounded = (value * SIX_DECIMAL_SCALE).round() / SIX_DECIMAL_SCALE;
263:     Ok(if rounded == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { rounded })
264: }
265: 
266: fn fixed_six_text(value: f64) -> Result<String, &'static str> {
267:     if !value.is_finite() {
268:         return Err("value must be finite");
269:     }
270: 
271:     Ok(format!("{value:.6}"))
272: }
273: ```
274: 
275: These helpers demonstrate separate operations; they do not establish TypeScript equivalence by themselves. JavaScript and Rust differ on rounding edge cases, negative zero, and number spelling. Each parity helper requires exhaustive fixtures generated by the pinned TypeScript oracle.
276: 
277: Never substitute one of the following without fixture evidence:
278: 
279: - `format!("{value:.6}")`
280: - `f64::to_string`
281: - A shortest-round-trip formatter
282: - `serde_json` number serialization
283: - `(value * scale).round() / scale`
284: 
285: ---
286: 
287: ## 3. IMPORT AND MODULE ORDERING
288: 
289: ### Import Group Order
290: 
291: Rust imports follow a three-group ordering with blank lines between groups:
292: 
293: ```rust
294: // 1. Standard library
295: use std::cmp::Ordering;
296: use std::collections::BTreeMap;
297: 
298: // 2. Third-party crates
299: use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
300: use thiserror::Error;
301: 
302: // 3. Current crate
303: use crate::error::CoreError;
304: use crate::ids::SymbolId;
305: ```
306: 
307: Within each group:
308: 
309: - Let `rustfmt` normalize brace layout.
310: - Sort imports lexically.
311: - Prefer one import tree per root where it remains readable.
312: - Do not use wildcard imports outside tightly scoped test preludes or established macro preludes.
313: - Keep trait imports visible when they enable methods whose origin would otherwise be unclear.
314: 
315: ### `self`, `super`, and `crate`
316: 
317: Use absolute `crate::` paths for ordinary cross-module imports. Use `super::` for parent-relative test or implementation details when the relationship is local and stable.
318: 
319: ```rust
320: use crate::error::CoreError;
321: use crate::ranking::RankedCandidate;
322: ```
323: 
324: Unit tests commonly import the module under test through `super`:
325: 
326: ```rust
327: #[cfg(test)]
328: mod tests {
329:     use super::{round_scaled_six, SIX_DECIMAL_SCALE};
330: 
331:     #[test]
332:     fn scale_is_six_decimal_places() {
333:         assert_eq!(SIX_DECIMAL_SCALE, 1_000_000.0);
334:         assert_eq!(round_scaled_six(1.0), Ok(1.0));
335:     }
336: }
337: ```
338: 
339: ### Module Declaration Order
340: 
341: Place module declarations after imports and before ordinary types or functions unless the crate root uses declarations as its primary index.
342: 
343: ```rust
344: mod dto;
345: mod error;
346: mod ids;
347: mod ranking;
348: 
349: pub use dto::{SearchOptions, SearchResult};
350: pub use error::CoreError;
351: pub use ids::SymbolId;
352: pub use ranking::rank_candidates;
353: ```
354: 
355: ### Re-Exports
356: 
357: Re-export only the intended stable surface.
358: 
359: ```rust
360: mod error;
361: mod ranking;
362: 
363: pub use error::CoreError;
364: pub use ranking::{rank_candidates, Candidate, RankedCandidate};
365: ```
366: 
367: Avoid:
368: 
369: ```rust
370: pub use ranking::*;
371: ```
372: 
373: Broad re-exports make accidental API growth difficult to detect and can expose adapter-internal types.
374: 
375: ### Macro Imports
376: 
377: Import derive macros and attributes explicitly:
378: 
379: ```rust
380: use napi_derive::napi;
381: use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
382: use thiserror::Error;
383: ```
384: 
385: Do not use `#[macro_use] extern crate ...` in modern Rust.
386: 
387: ### Conditional Imports
388: 
389: Keep target-specific imports close to the target-specific module. Prefer separate adapter crates. When conditional compilation is necessary, make it explicit:
390: 
391: ```rust
392: #[cfg(feature = "native")]
393: use napi::bindgen_prelude::Buffer;
394: 
395: #[cfg(feature = "wasm")]
396: use wasm_bindgen::prelude::JsValue;
397: ```
398: 
399: Do not conditionally import runtime values into the pure core.
400: 
401: ### Dependency Direction
402: 
403: The permitted dependency direction is:
404: 
405: ```text
406: napi adapter ─┐
407: wasm adapter ─┼──> pure core
408: sidecar ──────┘
409: ```
410: 
411: The pure core MUST NOT depend on:
412: 
413: - `napi`
414: - `napi-derive`
415: - `wasm-bindgen`
416: - `JsValue`
417: - Node handles
418: - WASM runtime handles
419: - Sidecar framing or process I/O
420: 
421: This protects the transport-neutral core contract and prevents runtime-specific behavior from changing deterministic algorithms.
422: 
423: ---
